summary: Comments on the proposed Initial Connection Protocol in RFC 123 and RFC 127. Bob Long at SDC noticed that the order messages leave depends on the local Network Control Program, so commands might go out before data. The user's NCP should keep the early requests until the data arrives.

eli5.summary: Two letters in a mail bag can leave in a different order than you wrote them. The note says the receiver should hold on to the early letter until the other arrives.

questions: why can icp messages arrive out of order
what did sdc notice about the icp
what layer violations did shoshani identify
why do different computers handle byte sizes differently
subtitle: Comments on protocol design issues in the Initial Connection Protocol

tldr.problem: Ari Shoshani at SDC noticed that the Initial Connection Protocol (RFC 123, 127) had issues with message ordering, byte size assumptions, and mixing of protocol layers that could cause interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: Shoshani documented three specific concerns: (1) message priority could cause initialization commands to arrive out of order, (2) the protocol mandated a 32-bit byte size that not all hosts could support, and (3) the protocol was making second-level Host-Host protocol decisions.
tldr.outcome: This feedback highlighted the need for careful consideration of implementation differences across network sites and proper separation between protocol layers.

today: RFC 151 updates RFC 127 and remains a historical record of early protocol design discussions. These issues influenced later thinking about protocol layer separation.

sections.title: Protocol Design Concerns
sections.content:
RFC 151 contains Ari Shoshani's critical comments on RFCs 123 and 127, which together proposed an official Initial Connection Protocol (ICP). Shoshani updates RFC 127, raising issues discovered during protocol review at SDC's NCP implementation.

The core problem: the sequence in which messages appear on the network depends on each site's local Network Control Program implementation, which can differ significantly. Commands might be sent before expected data, breaking protocol assumptions.
sections.eli5: Different computers organize their messages in different ways. One computer might send commands before data, which breaks the protocol that expects data first.

sections.title: Mixing Protocol Layers
sections.content:
Shoshani identifies three problems that violate the separation between the second-level Host-Host protocol and the third-level ICP. First, RFC 123 mandates a 32-bit byte size for server socket L, but the Host-Host protocol says the sender chooses the byte size (1 to 255 bits). Second, earlier RFCs required an ALL (allocation) before data transmission, but this requirement was removed in RFCs 123 and 127, creating a special case that some NCP implementations cannot handle. Third, comments about sending 32 bits in one message are a second-level decision that should not appear in a third-level protocol.

These violations create implementation headaches. For example, TIPs and other specialized hosts may not be prepared to receive or transmit messages in specific byte sizes.
sections.eli5: The protocol is trying to control low-level details that each computer should decide for itself. This means some computers cannot use the protocol.

sections.title: Implications for Implementation
sections.content:
Shoshani's feedback emphasizes that a third-level protocol should work with whatever the second level provides, not impose new restrictions. This is especially important for diverse hardware like TIPs, which have limited capabilities.

The protocol should remain flexible about byte sizes, message ordering, and low-level transmission details. Protocol designers need to think carefully about these implementation details before finalizing specifications.
sections.eli5: The protocol should be flexible enough to work with different types of computers, including small weak ones.
